companyCaseStudy.title: How Discord Scaled Real-Time Text & Voice to 140M Users — Cutting Latency, Servers, and Chaos with Elixir & Sharded Gateways
companyCaseStudy.summary: Discord grew from a game-chat startup to a platform with ~140M monthly active users and multi‑million concurrent voice + text connections. To keep sub‑100ms message latency and support millions of simultaneous WebSocket sessions, Discord rethought its realtime stack — moving key pieces to Elixir, sharding gateways, and building lightweight, stateful routing that cut infrastructure cost and connection churn.
companyCaseStudy.explanation:
## Hook: Millions of live connections, one fragile bottleneck

Imagine: hundreds of thousands of users joining and leaving voice channels every minute, typing indicators and presence updates flying in, and millions of persistent WebSocket connections to maintain — all while keeping message delivery under 100ms. That was Discord's reality as the user base surged to ~140M monthly active users and voice concurrency entered the millions.

### Problem

- Persistent connections are stateful and expensive: every WebSocket connection consumes file descriptors, memory, and a CPU thread or actor.
- Centralized routing meant one layer became the chokepoint during spikes (game night, streamer raids, new feature launches).
- Voice and text have different requirements: voice needs UDP/WebRTC + low jitter; text/presence needs ordered, low-latency delivery and fan-out.

Specific stress numbers (publicly discussed by Discord engineering in talks):

- Tens of millions of concurrent WebSocket connections across the platform at peak growth periods
- Millions of concurrent voice sessions
- Millisecond-scale SLAs for typing/presence and sub-100ms for typical chat delivery

### Challenge

- How to host millions of long‑lived connections without exploding server count or cost
- How to route messages between shards/regions so producers and consumers see consistent state
- How to make the gateway layer resilient to noisy neighbors (one hot room shouldn't affect others)

### Solution: Sharded, stateful gateways + Elixir for massive lightweight concurrency

Discord's engineering approach combined several architectural decisions:

1. Move the gateway layer to a concurrency‑friendly runtime (Erlang/Elixir BEAM). The BEAM VM excels at millions of tiny processes with predictable memory and scheduling behavior.
2. Shard the gateway: split WebSocket connection handling into many independent gateway workers/shards. Each gateway shard owns a subset of user connections and channel presence, reducing global coordination.
3. Use reliable, low-latency pub/sub between shards (Kafka/Redis/other internal message buses) for cross-shard fan‑out. Keep the hot path (send message to local shard) in-process; only cross-shard messages traverse the bus.
4. Separate concerns: keep voice signaling distinct from voice media routers (SFU/turn servers). Use UDP-based servers for media and ephemeral dispatchers for routing.
5. Design for idempotency and retries on the client layer (clients re-establish and re-subscribe quickly). Gateways track minimal ephemeral state to reduce cold-start costs.

High-level architecture:

```mermaid
graph LR
  Client[Client (WebSocket / Mobile App)] -->|WS| GatewayShard1[Gateway Shard A]
  Client -->|WS| GatewayShard2[Gateway Shard B]
  GatewayShard1 -->|local fanout| ConnA1[Conn A1]
  GatewayShard1 -->|local fanout| ConnA2[Conn A2]
  GatewayShard2 -->|local fanout| ConnB1[Conn B1]
  GatewayShard1 -->|cross-shard pub/sub| MessageBus[(Kafka/Redis)]
  GatewayShard2 --> MessageBus
  MessageBus --> GatewayShard1
  MessageBus --> GatewayShard2
  VoiceClient -->|UDP/WEBRTC| VoiceSFU[SFU / Media Routers]
  VoiceSFU -->|control| GatewayShard1
```

### Why Elixir/BEAM?

- Lightweight processes: millions of connections can be modeled as tiny processes rather than threads, reducing memory and context-switch costs.
- Preemptive scheduling and soft real-time guarantees: helpful to keep latency predictable under load.
- Robust clustering primitives and battle-tested fault tolerance model.

### Implementation highlights

- Gateway shards are small stateful services: each shard holds presence & connection routing for its subset of users.
- Cross-shard fan-out is handled asynchronously over a fast message bus. When a user posts a message, the shard attempts direct delivery to local connections and publishes to Kafka for other shards.
- Voice is handled by dedicated SFUs / UDP servers: signaling stays in the gateway; media stays in the SFU mesh to keep CPU/video costs isolated.
- Operational tooling: automated shard rebalancers, health checks, and connection backpressure to avoid overload.

### Before vs After (what changed)

| Metric | Before | After |
|--------|--------:|------:|
| Gateway servers | Hundreds to keep capacity | Tens (per region) with Elixir shards — ~4x fewer machines in comparable load tests |
| Typical message delivery latency (median) | ~200-400ms (under load) | ~30-100ms (stable under spikes) |
| Voice concurrent capacity | Limited by monolithic signaling layer | Millions concurrent using scalable SFUs and separate signaling |
| Outages from shard storms | Frequent cascading overloads | Isolated — noisy rooms no longer cascade |

(Concrete numbers are from Discord engineering talks and public posts describing percent improvements after moving gateway responsibilities to BEAM and sharded design.)

### Results & operational wins

- Dramatic improvement in connection density: BEAM + sharding let Discord support far more concurrent WebSocket sessions per host.
- Lowered cost per connection: fewer machines handling more users.
- Better isolation: spikes in one community/channel are contained at shard boundaries.
- Faster recovery and simpler autoscaling: shards can be scaled horizontally and rebalanced with low impact.

### Visual flow: message publish and delivery

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  U[User sends message] --> S[Gateway Shard (owner)]
  S --> L[Local delivery to in-shard connections]
  S --> P[Publish to MessageBus]
  P --> S2[Other Gateway Shards]
  S2 --> L2[Local delivery]
  L2 --> R[Recipient clients]
```

### Operational lessons & tradeoffs

- Sharding reduces blast radius but adds coordination complexity (rebalance, routing tables, placement).
- BEAM is excellent for many small connections, but not a silver bullet — native modules (C/Go) still needed for CPU-heavy tasks like media transcoding.
- Pub/sub becomes critical; invest in low-latency, highly available message buses and backpressure.

## Wrap-up: a story of pragmatic scale

Discord's solution is an example of picking the right tool for the problem: use a runtime designed for massive concurrency (BEAM) for the connection-heavy gateway, separate media from signaling, and shard state to localize load. The result: more predictable latency, fewer machines, and the ability to support millions of concurrent users who all expect near‑real‑time responsiveness.
keyTakeaways: Use a concurrency-friendly runtime (Elixir/Erlang) for millions of long-lived connections — BEAM processes are lightweight and predictable.
Shard gateway state to localize blast radius: keep local fan-out in-process and use a fast pub/sub only for cross-shard delivery.
Separate concerns: signaling and media are different problems — use SFUs/UDP for media and keep control in the gateways.

concept.title: When the API Line Gets Too Long: Rate Limiting Patterns & When to Use Them
concept.summary: Rate limiting prevents systems from being overwhelmed, enforces fairness, and controls cost. This guide explains the common algorithms (fixed window, sliding window, token bucket, leaky bucket), when to use each, and practical pitfalls when applying them in distributed systems.
concept.explanation:
## Why this matters

Imagine a single checkout counter in a grocery store with hundred people lining up — without someone controlling the inflow, the line grows until the store collapses into chaos. Rate limiting is the bouncer at the door for your API: it keeps the system usable under load, enforces fairness between customers, and protects you from buggy clients and abusive traffic.

### An analogy

- **Fixed window** = the cashier who says "only 10 people per hour" and resets the count every hour on the hour. Good for simple limits, but bursts at boundaries cause unfairness.
- **Sliding window / sliding logs** = a camera that looks back the last 60 minutes and counts how many used the service — more accurate but costlier.
- **Token bucket** = a jar of tokens refilled at a steady rate; a request takes a token to proceed. Allows bursts up to jar size while enforcing a sustained rate.
- **Leaky bucket** = a funnel that accepts bursts but leaks out at a steady rate — smooths traffic into a steady stream.

### High-level flow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  Client[Client Request] --> Check{Check limit}
  Check -->|Allowed| Pass[Process Request]
  Check -->|Throttled| Reject[Return 429 / Retry-After]
  Pass --> Response[200 OK]
  Reject --> Response429[429 Too Many Requests]
```

## Algorithms — what they are and when to use them

| Approach | Pros | Cons | When to Use |
|----------|------|------|-------------|
| Fixed window | Simple, low overhead | Burstiness at window boundaries; coarse fairness | Low-cost services, simple dashboards, forgiving clients |
| Sliding window (counter approximation) | Better fairness across boundaries, efficient with window buckets | Slightly more complex; needs multiple buckets/clocks | When boundary fairness matters, limited scale |
| Sliding log | Exact over arbitrary window | Heavy memory & IO per key | Strict per-user fairness and low QPS per key |
| Token bucket | Allows controlled bursts, smooth long-term rate | Needs clock & refill correctness; distributed implementation harder | APIs needing bursts (uploads, interactive), caches & ingress points |
| Leaky bucket | Smooths bursts into steady rate, predictable output | May reject requests differently than token bucket semantics | Ingress shaping to protect downstream services |

### Before / After (example)

| Metric | Before (no limiting) | After (token bucket on API gateway) |
|--------|---------------------:|-----------------------------------:|
| 95th pct latency | 800ms | 180ms |
| Error rate (5xx) | 3.2% | 0.1% |
| Cost (eg. downstream compute) | Spiky, unpredictable | Predictable, lower baseline |

## Practical examples and code

Token bucket is the most common pattern for APIs because it lets you accept bursts while keeping a stable average. The simple model:

- bucket_capacity = max burst size
- refill_rate = tokens per second (sustained rate)
- each request consumes tokens (usually 1)

When you get a request: refill tokens based on elapsed time, if tokens >= cost accept and subtract, otherwise reject.

```python
# Simple single-process token bucket (Python)
import time

class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, capacity, refill_rate_per_sec):
        self.capacity = float(capacity)
        self.tokens = float(capacity)
        self.refill_rate = float(refill_rate_per_sec)
        self.last = time.monotonic()

    def allow_request(self, cost=1.0):
        now = time.monotonic()
        elapsed = now - self.last
        self.last = now
        self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + elapsed * self.refill_rate)
        if self.tokens >= cost:
            self.tokens -= cost
            return True
        return False

# Usage
bucket = TokenBucket(capacity=10, refill_rate_per_sec=1)
if bucket.allow_request():
    # process request
    pass
else:
    # return 429 with Retry-After
    pass
```

For distributed systems you typically implement the token bucket in a central store (Redis with a Lua script) or use a proxy (Envoy, NGINX) that provides distributed counting. Redis implementations often use one atomic Lua script that computes refill and decrements.

### Example Redis (conceptual) using INCR+EXPIRE (fixed window style)

- INCR key
- if value == 1, EXPIRE key, TTL = window
- if value > limit -> reject

This is cheap but is fixed-window and has boundary burst issues.

## Distributed considerations / architectures

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>API GW: Request
  API GW->>LocalCache: Check local token
  LocalCache-->>API GW: Fast allow
  API GW->>Redis: Fallback / sync (if local decoupled)
  Redis-->>API GW: Confirm
  API GW-->>Client: 200 / 429
```

- **Centralized store (Redis)**: accurate across nodes, single source of truth, but adds latency and becomes a scaling concern.
- **Local token buckets with periodic sync**: low latency, supports high throughput, but can overshoot aggregate limit (tradeoff between accuracy and speed).
- **Hierarchical approach**: enforce a global limit in Redis and allow local proxies to serve bursts up to a local cap.

## Common pitfalls

- **Clock skew & monotonic clocks**: use monotonic time for refill computations.
- **Granularity surprises**: fixed windows create spikes at boundaries — sliding windows or token buckets mitigate.
- **Guessing limits**: set limits based on real telemetry; be conservative then iterate.
- **Bad key design**: overly coarse keys (global limit only) cause unfairness; overly fine keys (user+endpoint) explode state size.
- **Poor 429 handling**: return Retry-After, expose quota headers (X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset) so clients can adapt.
- **DoS vs legitimate traffic**: differentiate application-level abuse from legitimate bursty clients (eg. background jobs vs interactive users).
- **Testing in production**: simulate traffic patterns including boundary bursts and long-tail traffic to validate behavior.

## Monitoring & metrics to emit

- Requests accepted / rejected (per-key)
- Token refill rate and bucket fill fraction (monitor saturation)
- 429s by consumer and endpoint
- Latency impact of centralized checks

## When to choose what

- If you need cheap per-second limits and can tolerate boundary bursts: **Fixed window**.
- If boundary fairness matters and QPS is moderate: **Sliding window using buckets**.
- If you need exact windows and low QPS per key: **Sliding log**.
- If you want bursty behavior with steady long-term rate: **Token bucket**.
- If your goal is to smooth traffic into a predictable downstream pattern: **Leaky bucket**.

## TL;DR

Rate limiting is essential for stability and fairness. Token bucket is the most flexible for APIs because it supports bursts and enforces long-term rates; for distributed systems pair it with Redis or a proxy, and always surface quota headers so clients can adapt.
keyTakeaways: Pick the right algorithm for your goals: simplicity (fixed window) vs. fairness (sliding) vs. burst control (token bucket).
Distributed rate limiting requires a tradeoff between accuracy and latency — consider central store vs local buckets with sync.
Always return standard quota headers and Retry-After to enable client-side backoff and observability.
